title: Does ocean temperature affect giant kelp growth?
text:
Giant kelp (Macrocystis pyrifera) forests are among the most productive ecosystems on Earth, providing habitat and food for hundreds of species. As ocean temperatures rise due to climate change, understanding how temperature affects kelp growth is critical for predicting the future of these ecosystems.
In this project, I analyzed the relationship between ocean temperature (°C) and giant kelp frond elongation rate (cm day⁻¹) using correlation analysis.

title: Does ocean temperature affect giant kelp growth?
text:
Giant kelp (Macrocystis pyrifera) forests are among the most productive ecosystems on Earth, providing habitat and food for hundreds of species. As ocean temperatures rise due to climate change, understanding how temperature affects kelp growth is critical for predicting the future of these ecosystems.
In this project, I analyzed the relationship between ocean temperature (°C) and giant kelp frond elongation rate (cm day⁻¹) using correlation analysis.

title: Does ocean temperature affect giant kelp growth?
text:
The data
The dataset contains 32 observations of ocean temperature and kelp elongation rate from a field study.

library(tidyverse)
library(here)

# read in kelp data
kelp <- read_csv(here("data", "temp-kelp.csv"))

# preview the data
head(kelp)

# A tibble: 6 × 2
  temp_c kelp_elong
   <dbl>      <dbl>
1   19.2        6.5
2   16.3        6  
3   19.1        5.8
4   17.2        6.8
5   17.3        6.9
6   18.1        7.1

title: Does ocean temperature affect giant kelp growth?
text:
Visualization

ggplot(
  data = kelp,
  aes(x = temp_c, y = kelp_elong)
) +
  geom_point(color = "#a8d8a8", size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm", se = TRUE,
    color = "#E76F51", fill = "#E76F5133"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Ocean temperature (°C)",
    y = expression("Kelp elongation rate (cm day"^{-1}*")")
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent"),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent")
  )








The scatterplot shows a clear negative relationship: as temperature increases, kelp grows more slowly.

title: Does ocean temperature affect giant kelp growth?
text:
Statistical test
I used Pearson’s correlation coefficient because both variables are approximately normally distributed (Shapiro-Wilk p > 0.05) and the relationship appears linear.

# Pearson's correlation
kelp_pearson <- cor.test(
  x = kelp$temp_c,
  y = kelp$kelp_elong,
  method = "pearson"
)

kelp_pearson


    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  kelp$temp_c and kelp$kelp_elong
t = -5.189, df = 30, p-value = 1.366e-05
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.8359665 -0.4460157
sample estimates:
       cor 
-0.6877489

title: Does ocean temperature affect giant kelp growth?
text:
Results
There was a significant negative correlation between ocean temperature and kelp frond elongation rate (Pearson’s r = -0.69, p = 0). This means that as ocean temperatures increase, kelp grows more slowly — a concerning finding in the context of climate-driven ocean warming.

title: Does ocean temperature affect giant kelp growth?
text:
Why does this matter?
Kelp forests support thousands of species. Slower kelp growth means less habitat and food availability for fish, invertebrates, and marine mammals. As the ocean continues to warm, we may see significant declines in kelp forest health and extent along the California coast.

Dimension of Leachies (巨人维度) is my personal reptile hobby studio focused on keeping, studying, and sharing knowledge about Rhacodactylus leachianus — the leachianus gecko, or “leachie” — the largest gecko species in the world. The studio also works with a variety of other lizard species.
The name reflects both the impressive size of these animals (“giant” in Chinese: 巨人) and the layered, complex world of reptile keeping.

title: Dimension of Leachies
text:
The animals

Rhacodactylus leachianus — Leachianus gecko
Leachianus geckos are native to New Caledonia, a group of islands in the South Pacific. They are nocturnal, arboreal animals that can live for 20+ years in captivity. They’re known for their:

Impressive size — adults reach 25–35 cm and can weigh over 150g
Vocalizations — they produce growls, barks, and hisses unlike any other gecko
Personality — each animal has a distinct temperament, from docile to feisty
Stunning morphs — a wide range of natural color and pattern variations



Other species
In addition to leachies, the studio works with several other lizard species, including:

Crested geckos (Correlophus ciliatus)
Gargoyle geckos (Rhacodactylus auriculatus)
Other New Caledonian species

Providing enclosures that mimic natural habitat in size, structure, and climate
Feeding high-quality, varied diets
Minimizing unnecessary handling stress
Sourcing animals from reputable, ethical breeders

I believe that good husbandry is rooted in understanding the ecology of the animals in their native environment.

title: What makes my dog happiest? A personal data project
text:
As a dog owner, I’ve always wondered: what actually makes my dog most satisfied after a play session? Is it how long we play, whether he’s off-leash, or something else entirely?
To find out, I collected 42 days of data on my dog’s daily play sessions from April 17 to May 28, 2026, recording variables like playtime duration, leash status, weather, temperature, and my subjective rating of his satisfaction (1–5 scale) after each session.

title: What makes my dog happiest? A personal data project
text:
Does leash status affect satisfaction?

dog |>
  drop_na(leash_status, dog_satisfaction_level_1_5) |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = leash_status,
    y = dog_satisfaction_level_1_5,
    fill = leash_status
  )) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, height = 0.05, alpha = 0.7, size = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Off-leash" = "#a8d8a8", "On-leash" = "#F4A261")) +
  labs(
    x = "Leash status",
    y = "Dog satisfaction level (1–5)",
    subtitle = "Off-leash sessions are consistently more satisfying"
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








Off-leash sessions tend to produce higher and more consistent satisfaction scores. On-leash sessions show more variability, likely because other factors (playtime duration, weather) matter more when freedom is restricted.

title: What makes my dog happiest? A personal data project
text:
Does playtime duration matter?

dog |>
  drop_na(playtime_minutes, dog_satisfaction_level_1_5) |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = playtime_minutes,
    y = dog_satisfaction_level_1_5,
    color = leash_status
  )) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "grey60", linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Off-leash" = "#a8d8a8", "On-leash" = "#F4A261"),
    name = "Leash status"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Daily playtime (minutes)",
    y = "Dog satisfaction level (1–5)",
    subtitle = "Longer playtime is associated with higher satisfaction"
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.8, 0.25))

title: What makes my dog happiest? A personal data project
text:
What I learned
Both leash status and playtime duration are positively associated with my dog’s satisfaction. The data suggest that the best recipe for a happy dog is a long, off-leash session — ideally with other dogs present. This project taught me that personal data collection, even on something as simple as dog walks, can reveal meaningful patterns when collected consistently.

Breeding Lines

SHCGL — Super High Color Giant Line
The SHCGL line is selected for exceptionally vibrant coloration combined with large body size. Animals in this line display rich pink, orange, and green tones with high contrast patterning.





Two SHCGL individuals showing the characteristic high-contrast pink and green coloration.



Swirl Line
The Swirl line is selected for a distinctive swirling pattern across the dorsum. These animals show a blend of earth tones with flowing, irregular markings that give each individual a unique appearance.





Two Swirl line individuals showing the characteristic flowing pattern.



Goro Line — Melanistic Straight Line
The Goro line focuses on high melanin expression, producing animals with deep brown to near-black base coloration with subtle lighter spotting. This line is one of the most visually striking in the collection.





Two Goro line individuals displaying the characteristic dark, melanistic coloration.



Darth Maul Line
Named for its bold red-on-black patterning, the Darth Maul line is selected for deep red blotches against a dark background. These animals are among the most sought-after in the collection.





Two Darth Maul line individuals showing the signature red-on-dark coloration.

title: Spring Seasonal Change at Campus Point — UCSB Lagoon Field Study
text:
As part of ENVS 153 at UC Santa Barbara, our team conducted an 8-week field study tracking spring seasonal changes in vegetation, pollinators, and bird diversity at Campus Point — a coastal sage scrub and grassland site located next to Campus Point Beach, adjacent to UCSB’s Cheadle Center restoration area.
Team: Izzy Ribondo, Yaasiel Leos, and Zhelin Qi
Location: UCSB Campus Lagoon, Goleta, CA (34°24’22.7”N, 119°50’39.8”W)

title: Spring Seasonal Change at Campus Point — UCSB Lagoon Field Study
text:
As part of ENVS 153 at UC Santa Barbara, our team conducted an 8-week field study tracking spring seasonal changes in vegetation, pollinators, and bird diversity at Campus Point — a coastal sage scrub and grassland site located next to Campus Point Beach, adjacent to UCSB’s Cheadle Center restoration area.
Team: Izzy Ribondo, Yaasiel Leos, and Zhelin Qi
Location: UCSB Campus Lagoon, Goleta, CA (34°24’22.7”N, 119°50’39.8”W)

title: Spring Seasonal Change at Campus Point — UCSB Lagoon Field Study
text:
Why Campus Point?
We chose this site because of its rich ecological diversity and its position at the edge of the lagoon ecosystem. It offered:

High abundance of Wild Radish (Raphanus sativus) and Great Brome (Bromus diandrus) for tracking non-native plant changes
Presence of birds, pollinators, and lagoon wildlife
Proximity to the Cheadle Center coastal restoration area
A mix of native and non-native species expected to show rapid seasonal change through spring

A native Torrey Pine (Pinus torreyana) — one of North America’s rarest pine species — was also present at the site, supporting lichen growth and hummingbird nesting.

title: Spring Seasonal Change at Campus Point — UCSB Lagoon Field Study
text:
Research Questions
We investigated three main questions:
Q1: How does native and non-native vegetation change throughout the season near the lagoon at UCSB?
Q2: How does the increase in flowering plants affect pollinator abundance and activity near Campus Point?
Q3: How did bird species richness change throughout spring at Campus Point?

title: Spring Seasonal Change at Campus Point — UCSB Lagoon Field Study
text:
Methods
Every Thursday at 1:00 PM over 8 weeks, we visited the same site and recorded:

Temperature, weather, and site conditions
Bird species (identified with Merlin Bird ID)
Plant species and flower/seed counts (identified with Seek and iNaturalist)
5-minute pollinator surveys
Photos and timelapse documentation of site change

title: Spring Seasonal Change at Campus Point — UCSB Lagoon Field Study
text:
Results

Algae Coverage Over Time









Algae coverage ranged from 10% in Week 1 to a peak of 27% in Week 6, showing a general increasing trend through mid-season.



Pollinator Abundance Over Time









Pollinator abundance peaked at 13 per 5 minutes in Week 7, then dropped sharply to 2 in Week 8 as flowers senesced. Pollinators observed included Western Honeybees, cabbage white butterflies, and hummingbirds.



Great Brome Seeding Percentage









Great Brome seeding percentage declined from 70% in Week 2 to just 1% by Week 8, marking the completion of its reproductive cycle.



Flower and Seed Head Counts by Plant Species









Wild Radish dominated early in the season, peaking at over 436 flower/seed heads in Week 4 before declining sharply. Invasive species consistently outnumbered native species throughout the observation period.

title: Spring Seasonal Change at Campus Point — UCSB Lagoon Field Study
text:
Key Takeaways
This project gave me a firsthand look at how seasonal change drives cascading ecological effects — from plant phenology to insect activity to bird diversity. Watching the site transform week by week, from lush green vegetation in early spring to dry, seed-heavy grasses by late May, made abstract ecological concepts tangible. It also reinforced the impact of invasive species: Wild Radish and Great Brome consistently dominated the site, shaping the resources available to every other organism present.
